webTitle: Top Democrats set aside qualms and embrace progressive Abdul El-Sayed

fields.headline: Top Democrats set aside qualms and embrace progressive Abdul El-Sayed
fields.trailText: Democrats are ‘united by a common purpose,’ Chuck Schumer and Kirsten Gillibrand say in joint statement
fields.bodyText: Leading Democrats quickly papered over whatever qualms they had about progressive candidate Abdul El-Sayed after his win in the Michigan Senate primary was confirmed on Wednesday, instead welcoming the former public health official as their champion against the Republican nominee, Mike Rogers. The state is now key to Democrats’s hopes of retaking control of the chamber in November’s midterm elections. Winning in Michigan would put them on the path to snarling Donald Trump’s legislative agenda and blocking his judicial nominees for the final two years of his presidency, while defeat could undermine their prospects of gaining a majority in the chamber for years to come. Rogers lost a Senate race in Michigan two years ago by a slim margin to Democrat Elissa Slotkin. “Democrats are united by a common purpose: putting a check on Donald Trump by defeating his Republican enablers and taking back the Senate. We look forward to working with Abdul and Democrats across Michigan to win this seat in November,” the Senate minority leader, Chuck Schumer, and Kirsten Gillibrand, who chairs the Democratic Senate campaign arm, said in a joint statement. Schumer was among a long list of Democratic establishment figures who had rallied behind Stevens in the weeks before the vote, as polls showed her trailing El-Sayed. He ultimately prevailed but by a far slimmer margin than data indicated, winning by 48.5% to Stevens’s 47.5%. “There’s a lot of passion and energy in these primaries, and that’s a good thing. Democrats are ready to beat Republicans across the state,” said Governor Gretchen Whitmer, who had endorsed Stevens. “We’re all united by our shared goal of getting things done for the people in Michigan.” The easiest path for Democrats to win back the Senate – which Republicans control with 53 lawmakers to their 47 – requires holding on to their seats in Michigan and Georgia while ousting Republicans from blue state Maine as well as three other red states. Democratic leaders believe they have the right candidates to pull that off in North Carolina, Ohio and Alaska, but it will nonetheless be a tall order, given that all three states backed Trump in 2024, and the latter two by double-digit margins. Michigan’s Democratic senator Gary Peters, whose decision not to seek re-election had sparked the primary for his seat, backed Stevens as his replacement but quickly endorsed El-Sayed after his primary. “Both candidates ran strong campaigns focused on improving the lives of all Michiganders. But now it’s time to come together as a party and rally around our nominee, Abdul El-Sayed, to make sure Mike Rogers never sees the floor of the US Senate,” Peters said. In a statement released following her loss, Stevens congratulated El-Sayed but did not outright endorse him, instead indicating she was ready to campaign for him as well as Democrats vying to win swing districts in Michigan. “This was a thorough and rigorous campaign that brought out the full span of views within the Democratic party – and that is why we have primaries. I am proud to have put up my hand to serve, and prouder to continue to work together to make sure this Senate seat remains blue, that we flip the United States Senate and continue the work for Michigan,” Stevens said. Republicans meanwhile pounced on El-Sayed’s views to paint him as too far left for voters in Michigan, a state that backed Trump in 2016 and again in 2024. “The choice this November is simple: common sense or complete insanity,” Rogers said. The former congressman blamed Democrats – who have held both of Michigan’s Senate seats since 2001 – for job losses in manufacturing, while saying El-Sayed “doesn’t represent a vision for the future. He’s leading a movement grounded in ideological fanaticism.” The question of aid to Israel animated the primary, with Stevens arguing Democrats should continue backing the US’s top ally in the Middle East and El-Sayed calling for an end to military support in response to its actions in Gaza and the West Bank. The United Democracy Project, a Super Pac connected to the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (Aipac), spent more than $30m in the race to support Stevens and oppose El-Sayed, to no avail, and he now joins others in Denver, New York City, New Jersey and Philadelphia in having wooed Democratic voters in part by vowing to stand up for Palestinian rights. “Abdul’s victory is a win for everyone who supports equality, justice, and a thriving future for all,” said the IfNotNow Movement, a Jewish organization opposed to Israel’s policy towards Palestinians. “We urge those who see Abdul’s support for Palestinian human rights and blocking weapons to Israel as a threat to our community to reconsider. It is incredibly dangerous to conflate Jewish safety with support for Aipac or Israel’s military.” Brian Romick, president of the Democratic Majority for Israel Pac, called El-Sayed’s victory an indicator that “there is clearly strong anti-establishment energy this cycle, but no one should count pro-Israel Democrats out”. “While El-Sayed’s razor-thin victory in Michigan is disappointing, it was hardly the sweeping triumph he predicted or a mandate for his views,” Romick said, noting that Stevens lost only narrowly.

webTitle: Morning Mail: First home buyers’ scheme twist; explosive drone scare at German airport; butterflies on the move

fields.headline: Morning Mail: First home buyers’ scheme twist; explosive drone scare at German airport; butterflies on the move
fields.trailText: Homes bought under 5% deposit scheme turned into investments; drone carrying explosives found in Leipzig
fields.bodyText: Good morning. Nearly 1,500 properties bought using the government’s first home buyers’ 5% deposit scheme have ended up being converted into investments: we dig into the data to find out more. A drone carrying explosives was found at a German airport. Meanwhile, Ukraine is pleading with its allies for more air defences after Russia pounded Kyiv with ballistic missiles. Scientists are excited by new pictures of the sun, but worried by the migration of butterflies. And a poll has placed Cathy Freeman at the top of a list of Australia’s most admired sportspeople. Australia Operation Richmond | A new report has highlighted how – via a “staged” meeting and a secret deal – a union boss exerted “extraordinary influence” on the Daniel Andrews government in Victoria. ‘It shouldn’t benefit the wealthy’ | The government’s 5% deposit scheme for first home buyers has enabled the purchase of almost 1,500 properties that were turned into investments, data shows. ‘Easy cash grab’ | Jetstar’s new carry-on luggage charge means the airline has joined a growing number monetising basic services in the sky. And: what’s one more humiliating ritual for the masses, James Colley asks. Analysis | Ex-NSW premier Dominic Perrottet’s brother Jean-Claude was the star witness at the Icac hearings yesterday. It won’t be the last we hear from his family, Anne Davies writes. Datacentre stoush | The energy minister, Chris Bowen, has vowed to override states opposing national rules that new AI datacentres are to be powered by renewable energy and not fuelled by gas. World Russia-Ukraine war | Volodymyr Zelenskyy has blamed allies for not delivering air defences fast enough after Ukraine failed to shoot down a single Russian missile in a deadly overnight attack. Drone scare | German police deployed a bomb disposal robot after a drone carrying explosives was found at Leipzig airport, causing alarm and the diversion of several flights; the Leipzig drone bomb marks a dangerous escalation for Europe, Dan Sabbagh writes. A defining race? | Abdul El-Sayed has won the Democratic primary for US Senate in Michigan; top Democrats are now setting aside their qualms to embrace the progressive leftwing candidate. Middle East crisis | Iran says it has agreed the coordinates of a shipping route through the strait of Hormuz with Oman. An Israeli airstrike in south Lebanon has killed one person and injured 11. Science | Butterflies around the world are on the move, and their migration reveals the impact of climate change. In other news, scientists are very excited by new high-res photos of the sun. Full Story Decoding America: are the Democrats having their own Maga moment? In our weekly US politics podcast, Jonathan Yerushalmy and Reged Ahmad look at how the Michigan Senate primaries could decide the future of the Democrats. The race has revealed the civil war raging inside the party, as some seek to take it further to the left. Will this schism be the Democrats’ Maga moment, or could it cost them in the midterms? In-depth The Reserve Bank governor, Michele Bullock, says rate rises don’t really increase living costs. But the latest data is clear – they very much do. Economics and finance are purposefully confusing but, Greg Jericho writes, people are well aware of how rate hikes affect them. Not the news For her new book, It’s Not For You, the Camp Cope bassist Kelly-Dawn Hellmrich interviewed 18 women and gender-diverse artists who have changed the Australian music industry on their own terms, including Amy Taylor, Marcia Hines and Courtney Barnett. The book opens up topics such as motherhood, abuse and respect – and is intended, she says, “for every artist who felt pushed away, or talked over”. Sport Sporting poll | Cathy Freeman leads a trio of women at the top of a list of Australia’s most admired sportspeople, with Ash Barty and Sam Kerr coming joint second. Rugby league | The UK Super League is closing in on a gamechanging investment from Australia’s NRL. Football | “Fifa Super League”: Gianni Infantino discussed having the governing body’s name on an ill-fated European breakaway; why has football taken so long to rebel against Fifa, Jonathan Liew asks. And: Mohamed Salah has landed in Turkey to sign for Trabzonspor. Cycling | Demi Vollering was victorious on stage five of the Tour de France Femmes as Pauline Ferrand-Prévot’s defence unravelled. Golf | LIV Golf says it has secured a “lead investor” until 2030 – but the future of star names still remains uncertain. Media roundup Crew members on Carnival cruise ships have made “horrifying” allegations about their working conditions in an ABC News investigation. Kidnapping has emerged as a major escalation of the violence used in the so-called tobacco war, the Age reports. Documents reveal that taxpayers shelled out for a $50,000-a-year Tasmanian electorate office that nobody ever used, the Mercury reports. What’s happening today WA | A public hearing is scheduled in the inquiry into the NDIS amendment bill in Perth. NSW | The trial of Alan Jones continues in Sydney. NSW | Public hearings in the royal commission on antisemitism and social cohesion continue in Sydney. ABS | The Australian Bureau of Statistics is scheduled to release its latest international trade in goods figures. webTitle: What we learned from midterm primary elections in five key states

fields.headline: What we learned from midterm primary elections in five key states
fields.trailText: Elections underscored that momentum of progressive candidates remains strong but not unstoppable
fields.bodyText: Tuesday’s primary elections in five states will be looked back on as a marquee moment ahead of November’s midterm elections, as voters in Michigan, Washington, Virginia, Kansas and Missouri selected candidates for races that could decide which party wins control of Congress. Here’s a rundown of what we learned from the results: Progressives thought their Michigan Senate candidate would be a shoo-in – but his victory was narrow Michigan was the site of a bitterly contested Democratic Senate primary in which the moderate congresswoman Haley Stevens faced former public health official Abdul El-Sayed, a progressive, in a state that Donald Trump won two years ago. Ahead of Tuesday’s vote, polls showed El-Sayed with a firm lead over Stevens, who had the backing of Governor Gretchen Whitmer as well as the top Senate Democrat, Chuck Schumer, and his campaign projected confidence accordingly. But the election turned out to be a squeaker, with El-Sayed winning 48.5% of the vote to Stevens’s 47.5%, the Associated Press reports, far from the blowout polling appeared to show. Republicans nominated former congressman Mike Rogers, who narrowly lost the race for the state’s other Senate seat two years ago. The left’s momentum remains strong … El-Sayed’s victory underscored the continued momentum of progressive candidates, who have been on a roll in primaries in New York and Colorado as they harnessed discontent among Democrats with party leadership and their traditional support for Israel. Adding to the movement’s trophies was William Lawrence, the co-founder of the climate change activist group the Sunrise Movement, who clinched the Democratic nomination for the battleground seventh congressional district in central Michigan. In Detroit, progressive Donavan McKinney succeeded in ousting Congressman Shri Thanedar, who had been backed by groups aligned with the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (Aipac). … but not unstoppable Leftwing challengers did not triumph everywhere. In Missouri, voters in the St Louis area rejected former congresswoman Cori Bush’s attempt at a political comeback and renominated the incumbent Wesley Bell, who unseated her two years ago with the help of spending from pro-Israel groups. Bush, a progressive who believes the US ally committed a genocide in Gaza, attempted to harness dislike of Israel among primary voters to her advantage against Bell, who received heavy backing from an Aipac-linked Super Pac. But she lost badly, receiving not even 40% of the vote. In Washington, Congresswoman Marie Gluesenkamp Perez, one of the few Democrats holding on to a district that Trump won two years ago, clinched her primary against a crowded field that included a challenger to her left. Republicans asked too much of their own voters Missouri’s Republican leaders had backed a ballot initiative that would have made it more difficult for state constitutional amendments to pass, after their voters in recent years approved abortion protections, paid sick leave and cannabis legalization at the ballot box. That measure was rejected by a whopping 80% vote, as was an attempt to phase out the state income tax, by a similarly huge margin. And four years after voters in heavily Republican Kansas approved abortion protections in the state constitution, they turned back a GOP-backed attempt to have state supreme court judges popularly elected rather than appointed by the governor. The current bench had attracted Republican ire for issuing rulings against the party’s interests, including on abortion rights. Democrats in battleground Michigan are split all kinds of ways Michigan’s Democratic voters chose their fighters in Tuesday’s primary for a Senate race that could determine whether the party returns to the majority in the chamber, as well as for vital House races. But the primaries also underscored sharp divides among their backers over which brand of the Democratic party works best for them. Stevens’s strong primary performance shows El-Sayed has work to do to win over the centrist voters she courted, as well as those who preferred her views on Israel. The task is much the same for Lawrence, who triumphed over a divided field of moderate Democrats but now must convince voters to get on board with his progressive politics in a district that’s one of the most narrowly divided in the country.

webTitle: Abdul El-Sayed’s win proves change is possible for Democrats. His next fight may determine their future

fields.headline: Abdul El-Sayed’s win proves change is possible for Democrats. His next fight may determine their future
fields.trailText: If the progressive wins Michigan’s general election, it could redefine the 2028 presidential contest. If he fails, the establishment will call him a cautionary tale
fields.bodyText: In the final stretch of the state’s Democratic primary for US Senate, Abdul El-Sayed challenged voters at a small event in rural Michigan to think about the message they could send the rest of the country when they cast their ballots. “Who are we? Who do we want to be?” El-Sayed said. “Do we want a state that’s defined by how much money corporations brought in to tell us what we couldn’t have? Or do we want to be a state where we demonstrate to the rest of the country what’s possible when you build a movement of, by and for the people?” On Tuesday, El-Sayed’s vision cleared its first hurdle: he won the primary over moderate congresswoman Haley Stevens, who was backed by the party’s establishment, and tens of millions of dollars in outside spending. His rise, and victory, could serve as a revision to how the political establishment views swing-state politics – not requiring candidates to run from the center, but articulating how you will materially improve people’s lives as the working and middle classes struggle with affordability and rising healthcare costs. A contentious general election, in a battleground state, awaits. El-Sayed led by 48.5% to 47.5% over Stevens when the race was called. The narrow margin, in addition to more than 60,000 votes for a candidate who dropped out altogether, suggest he will have to unite the party, and convince more independent and even right-leaning voters in a swing state, to beat Republican Mike Rogers. But the race solidified a growing anti-establishment sentiment on the party’s left, where activists and supporters have sought a proactive vision that doesn’t rely on the pre-Trump status quo, apparent in a string of wins for insurgent candidates. There’s a sense that systems were already broken before Trump’s rise, and a return to those norms won’t serve everyday Americans. They’re looking for politicians who can call out their own party’s orthodoxies, and challenge the big money that haunts US politics. Michigan voters found it in El-Sayed, who centered his campaign around universal healthcare, and wasn’t shy about calling the war in Gaza a genocide. “It doesn’t limit us to just what we think is possible, but it changes what we think is possible,” said David Sernick, a voter in Detroit who supported El-Sayed. El-Sayed first ran for office in 2018, losing to Gretchen Whitmer, now the governor of Michigan, in a Democratic primary. This time, he built a grassroots machine, barnstorming the state with in-person rallies while delivering clippable moments for social media feeds. His campaign knocked on more than 200,000 doors and made more than 1m phone calls, aided by leftwing groups such as the Working Families party and Indivisible chapters. El-Sayed held more than 500 campaign events and visited 150 churches. People like Racquel Garcia, who voted for El-Sayed in Dearborn, Michigan, said his willingness to show up underpinned their vote. El-Sayed worked as a public health official in Detroit and in Wayne county, and would show up at permit hearings and represent the people, she said. “Every time we meet with the city of Detroit officials, we’re like, ‘we need you to be like him’,” said Garcia. “You’re here to protect us, not to protect industry. So we’ve been wanting him in office. We were happy that he’s real.” Andy Levin, a former congressman from Michigan who lost to Stevens in 2022 after their districts were redrawn, said the moment rejected a “static notion of electability” that stems from a politics of anxiety and fear. “They want authenticity, they want truth telling and they want brave policy, not just proposals but action, so they can breathe in their lives,” Levin told Democracy Now. “This is a movement of Americans who are saying, enough of politics as usual.” Roy Harris, who voted in Detroit on Tuesday but wouldn’t say for whom, detailed how it was time for a change. “First-time homebuyers can’t buy a house – $400,000, first time you going out, nobody can afford that,” he said. “I’m tired of paying $4 for gas, and I am looking for a change. And I hope the new regime coming in brings that to us.” In Washington, El-Sayed’s effort to win the US Senate race in Michigan is critical for Democrats’ ambitious hopes of retaking control of the upper chamber, and will be closely watched by all factions of the left as a bellwether for the party’s future. Michigan voted for Trump, then Biden, and then Trump, in presidential elections. It is firmly a swing state. If El-Sayed, an unabashed progressive who frequently notes he has a “funny name”, can win a statewide general election, it could remake the contours of the 2028 presidential contest. If he fails, the establishment and pundit class will call him, and his ideas, too extreme – a cautionary tale for play-it-safe politics. In other parts of the country, moderates won their Democratic primaries, including blue-dog Democrat Marie Gluesenkamp Perez in a purple district in Washington state, who staved off a progressive challenge, and Wesley Bell, who saw off a challenge from Cori Bush, a former representative. Chris Rabb, a progressive who won a contested primary for a US congressional seat in Pennsylvania, recently noted the high bar people from his branch of the party face as they seek to challenge moderates. “Nobody asks ‘centrist’ Dems to explain their losses,” Rabb wrote on X. “They lose purple districts every cycle & Beltway pundits call it ‘a tough map’. Progressives lose one major race & Dem operatives call us electoral pariahs. It’s a specious double standard.” Meanwhile, the attack lines from the right have already been drawn. Rogers posted an AI-generated video of El-Sayed, depicting him as Odysseus among other prominent Democrats inside a Trojan horse, and saying “don’t let communism into Michigan”. A Republican has not won a US Senate seat in Michigan since 1994. The Republican National Committee called El-Sayed “Michigan’s Mamdani” and said the race “pits common sense against crazy”. El-Sayed himself remains confident. In November, he is counting on turning out people who normally turn off from politics because they’re cynical, or believe the system cannot change in a way that would make their lives better. “The goal now is not to dunk on anybody, the goal now is to come together so we can all collectively dunk on Mike Rogers,” El-Sayed said.

webTitle: Abdul El-Sayed wins Michigan Senate primary in defining race for Democrats

fields.headline: Abdul El-Sayed wins Michigan Senate primary in defining race for Democrats
fields.trailText: Progressive candidate will face Republican Mike Rogers in race to represent midwestern purple state in the Senate
fields.bodyText: Abdul El-Sayed won the Democratic primary for US Senate in Michigan, becoming the latest leftwing candidate to capture the party’s nomination ahead of November’s midterm elections. El-Sayed, a progressive, beat Haley Stevens, a moderate US representative backed by the party’s establishment. He will now face Republican Mike Rogers in the race to represent the midwestern purple state in the Senate. The Associated Press called the race on Wednesday morning, moments after Stevens’s campaign said she had called El-Sayed to concede. El-Sayed succeeded by a relatively close margin, in a sign that battleground state voters are still grappling over the direction of the Democratic party. Michigan voters also delivered victories for other progressive candidates, nominating climate activist William Lawrence and Donavan McKinney, a member of the Democratic Socialists of America, both of whom are backed by Bernie Sanders in their bids for seats in the House of Representatives. Donald Trump won Michigan in 2016 and 2024, though Joe Biden won it in 2020. Both the state’s current senators are Democrats and retaining the seat remains critical to Democrats’ hopes of winning back the US Senate this year, and a crucial part of the map for the 2028 presidential election. El-Sayed, 41, is a former public health official who centered his run on the Medicare for All model of universal healthcare, while confronting heavy outside spending against him, which became another theme of the race. Stevens, meanwhile, touted her work on the US auto rescue taskforce, where she served as chief of staff. Rogers, a former congressman from the state, was also the Republican nominee for US Senate in 2024, when he lost to the senator Elissa Slotkin. Should he win in November, and beat Rogers in the general election in Michigan, El-Sayed could become the first Muslim US senator. While he is not a democratic socialist, his primary win came amid a wave of wins by democratic socialist candidates elsewhere in the country. He has said he is a “capitalist who understands how capitalism works”, and who wants to regulate monopolies. “They spent an unprecedented amount of money to beat us,” El-Sayed said at a press conference on Wednesday, referring to the tens of millions of dollars in spending against him. “But it turns out the commercials are the part of the television show most people don’t want to watch. “We took on a machine. You’re not supposed to be able to beat $70m of outside spending, a record amount of money spent in a campaign against a Democrat in a primary, in any campaign. You’re not supposed to be able to beat that. And what we showed is that the power of our many is greater than the power of their money.” Stevens saw the backing of establishment Democrats, including Chuck Schumer, the Senate minority leader, while El-Sayed received endorsements from prominent progressives such as Sanders. In a statement on Wednesday, Stevens said: “I love Michigan and am so proud to have put up my hand to serve. I spoke with Abdul a few moments ago to offer him my full support as we work to defeat Mike Rogers this November.” Until earlier this summer, the race was a three-way race with Mallory McMorrow, a state senator who eventually dropped out. Early Wednesday, McMorrow threw her support behind El-Sayed. “I’m proud to give Abdul my full endorsement and support as we head to November together as a unified party,” she said in a statement. The role of Black voters in the Democratic primary came into focus in the final weeks of campaigning, with both candidates seeking to turn out the vote in Black communities, which make up about one-fifth of the Democratic primary electorate, via events at churches and festivals. More than $40m poured into the race from outside groups supporting Stevens or attacking El-Sayed, including from groups associated with the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (Aipac), a pro-Israel lobby. Some ads elevated Stevens’s connection to Barack Obama on the auto rescue, which voters have seen as a quasi-endorsement, despite Obama not formally endorsing in the race. Trump celebrated El-Sayed’s victory on Tuesday, claiming it was “great news” for Republicans in a post on his Truth Social platform. The president went on to call El-Sayed a “communist loser who hates Jews and Israel”, despite the Democratic nominee’s frequent denunciations of antisemitism. “Now, the Dumocrats crazy policies will only get worse!” Trump wrote. Shortly after 1am, when the race remained too close to call, El-Sayed took the stage at Detroit’s Majestic Theater to Tupac Shakur’s Changes, telling hundreds of supporters to stay patient as the votes were being counted. Instead, he cast his contest with Stevens as proof that a grassroots campaign could compete against unprecedented outside spending. “We’re still standing,” he told the raucous crowd, arguing Michigan voters were motivated less by ideological divides than by the rising cost of rent, groceries and healthcare. The political streamer Hasan Piker, the democratic nominee for Philadelphia’s third district, Chris Rabb, and Colorado Democratic nominee, Melat Kiros, were in the room. Rabb said he believed El-Sayed’s campaign reflected a broader shift inside the Democratic party, pointing to recent victories by progressive candidates including Zohran Mamdani in New York and Adam Hamawy in New Jersey. “This is not just among coastal elites,” Rabb said. “That’s something that could benefit Democrats if they have the collective wisdom to move us forward, not left or right. Because if they don’t learn this lesson, it’ll be through all of our defeats.” More than 1.2 million Michiganders cast ballots before election day, including nearly 139,000 who voted during the state’s nine-day early in-person voting period, a number that doubles 2024’s primary, according to the Michigan department of state. Rabb argued that unusually strong early turnout suggested the campaign was expanding the Democratic coalition rather than simply energizing existing voters. He said voters were turning out “because they believe in this brother”, adding that Democrats should see the result as evidence that “our base is radically expanding to folks who have not been seen, heard, or respected”. During his speech in the early hours of Wednesday, El-Sayed sought to lower the temperature of the bitter primary, calling on his supporters to unite behind the eventual Democratic nominee against Rogers. “Tomorrow we begin to mend fences,” he said. “There is so much more that unites us than divides us.”

webTitle: The Democratic party chair is a handy scapegoat. But the party’s problems are much bigger | Norman Solomon

fields.headline: The Democratic party chair is a handy scapegoat. But the party’s problems are much bigger
fields.trailText: Much of the criticism of Ken Martin is deserved. But his actions are symptomatic of a party that fails to listen to the grassroots
fields.bodyText: Ken Martin is now a convenient scapegoat. As chair of the Democratic National Committee, he has stumbled into disrepute as a dubious fundraiser and bad-tempered boss who bungled an autopsy report on the 2024 election disaster. Much of the criticism is justified. But Martin is just a symptom of what deeply ails a party that does not live up to its name. As the Democratic party’s governing body, the Democratic National Committee has long operated as a fortress for party elites who expect to get their way. Martin seemed to offer a bit of a departure when, as Minnesota party chair, he won the committee leadership election last year in part because of his close ties with other state party chairs. They remain among his strongest supporters. That’s one reason why Martin is very well-positioned to fend off any challenge to his hold on power when the full committee meets next week in Austin. But a more basic dynamic protecting Martin is the committee’s internal culture of conformity. Most of its 450 members would not dream of publicly challenging the chair, despite the recent torrent of bad press. News media have hammered on the fact that the DNC is $2.2m in debt while the Republican National Committee reports $128m in cash on hand. Yet depictions of the DNC’s financial woes have given short shrift to some relevant factors. For instance, after Kamala Harris spent $1.5bn during her short presidential campaign in 2024, the DNC took on about $22m in debts that she left behind. Martin has fulfilled his promise to send more money to state parties. In April 2025, the DNC announced: “Each state party will receive a baseline of $17,500 a month, a $5,000 per month increase over the last agreement, and Republican-controlled states will receive an additional investment of $5,000 a month.” What happens to that no-strings money, however, is a whole other question. “When we’re talking about giving tens of thousands of dollars away on a monthly basis, we need to know that it’s going towards real, grassroots organizing,” Chris Davis, the president of Colorado Young Democrats, told me. “Money received by each state party from the DNC needs to be tied to deliverables that will directly grow the party, such as direct voter engagement through canvassing, having a presence in community spaces like tabling on college campuses or large community gatherings, or building the party’s following through organic social media engagement. Otherwise, the money could be going to consultants, for all we know.” The prevailing criticism is that Martin has failed to take full advantage of the party’s biggest donors and fundraisers. The emphasis on the importance of well-heeled patrons is telling. It says a lot about prevailing assumptions that the party should be largely dependent on – and responsive to – the rich. The DNC’s business model involves catering to – and relying on – big donors. A current somber refrain from news media and some party operatives is that Martin has lost the confidence of party backers who can write big checks. His response, in an essay posted on 20 July, underlines the problem. Martin trumpeted success with “grassroots donors” – whom he defined as people giving “under $10,000”. And he touted an upsurge in funding from the super wealthy during the last year and a half, writing: “The current DNC secured contributions of $100,000 or more from 67 donors.” Rarely mentioned is the truth that he and other party leaders have lost the confidence of countless small-dollar donors, who’ve shown ample capacity to provide fully adequate national funding hauls if inspired, as during the 2016 and 2020 Bernie Sanders presidential campaigns. But it would be hard to find more uninspiring Democratic leaders than the party’s most visible and powerful ones, Senator Chuck Schumer and Representative Hakeem Jeffries. Although Schumer and Jeffries did not support Martin’s run for DNC chair in early 2025, the three share a top-down approach that sticks to the party’s standard positions on key issues, even when those positions are in sync with only a minority of Democrats or voters overall. Party leaders are hardly in a good position to effectively raise money from the Democratic base while continuing to flagrantly oppose what polls show the base overwhelmingly wants, such as major tax hikes on the wealthy and an arms embargo on Israel. Journalists have been vastly more fascinated by Martin reportedly throwing a cellphone at a DNC employee’s desk than how he has blocked any DNC resolution for halting US arms shipments to Israel that enable deadly attacks on Palestinian civilians in Gaza. The ingrained habit of deferring to a DNC chair makes a course correction unlikely in the next few months. But all bets are off after the midterm elections in early November. Conjecture is already widespread about who might replace Martin next winter. One of the names cropping up as a possibility in mainstream media is Donna Brazile, whose second stint as interim chair of the committee began in mid-2016. Later that year, she was fired as a CNN commentator after the revelation that she had shared debate questions with Hillary Clinton’s presidential campaign to aid her performance against Sanders. In a Washington Post op-ed last week, Brazile argued that Martin “should keep his job”. The piece was ostensibly focused on unifying her party to defeat Republicans this fall, but Brazile slipped in a battle cry on behalf of the corporate Democrats circling Martin’s blood in the political water. “Democrats can win control of both houses of Congress in the midterms by rallying around what unites them,” Brazile wrote. “By advocating for pragmatic policies that most Americans support to make our country more affordable, rather than extremist socialist policies that most voters oppose.” But the momentum of democratic socialists and other progressives in primary elections this year offers real possibilities for transforming the party from the grassroots up – to end the reign of unaccountable authority from the top down. Norman Solomon is the director of RootsAction and executive director of the Institute for Public Accuracy. His latest book is The Blue Road to Trump Hell: How Corporate Democrats Paved the Way for Autocracy

webTitle: Republican Chuck Edwards drops bid for re-election after report finding sexual harassment of staffers

fields.headline: Republican Chuck Edwards drops bid for re-election after report finding sexual harassment of staffers
fields.trailText: Congressional ethics panel had recommended Edwards face censure over its findings on ‘hostile work environment’
fields.bodyText: Chuck Edwards announced he would not run for re-election after the US House of Representatives ethics committee determined the US congressman “fostered a hostile work environment and engaged in sexual harassment” by giving gifts and lavishing attention on two young female staffers. Edwards, a Republican for North Carolina, said he would complete his current term, which is due to end in January. In a statement posted on social media early on Wednesday morning, Edwards said: “After much prayer and reflection, I’ve decided to withdraw from my re-election campaign. I will complete my current term. Serving western North Carolina has been the honor of my life. Thank you for your trust, prayers, and support.” The bipartisan congressional ethics panel recommended on Monday that Edwards face censure over its findings. Should the House agree, he will have to stand in the well of the chamber while the text of a resolution rebuking him is read aloud. The ethics committee launched an investigation into Edwards earlier this year, after receiving complaints about his conduct. In a report approved by Democratic and Republican committee members, it said there was “substantial reason to believe” that Edwards had broken House rules by singling out the two unidentified aides for special treatment that made them uncomfortable and harmed relations with other employees. While the investigation uncovered no evidence that Edwards engaged in sexual activity with the staffers or suggested it, his behavior probably violated provisions in the House code of conduct that prohibit sexual harassment and unwanted advances. The congressman “acknowledged at least some of the behavior at issue could be viewed as inappropriate”, but “has not acknowledged or taken responsibility for the harm he caused”, the committee wrote in its report. Edwards was already viewed as vulnerable to losing re-election to his western North Carolina district in the November midterm elections. Last week the election forecaster Sabato’s Crystal Ball announced it was rating his race a “toss-up”, in a sign of improving Democratic chances.

webTitle: Let’s call Trump’s approach to Iran what it is: kindergarten diplomacy | Moustafa Bayoumi

fields.headline: Let’s call Trump’s approach to Iran what it is: kindergarten diplomacy
fields.trailText: Amid stop-and-start threats and with a divided staff, it’s clear Trump has no idea how to end a war that shouldn’t have begun
fields.bodyText: On Thursday, 23 July, after weeks of escalating attacks between the US and Iran, Donald Trump told a reporter that Iran hadn’t received “enough pain yet”, and he leveled a threat. “I am considering a massive attack. Bigger than ever before,” he warned. “I am close to making a decision.” Then, on Monday 27 July, he called it off. A few days later, on Friday 31 July, Trump said: “We’ll be hitting them very hard. At some point, they’re going to say: ‘We just can’t take it any more.’” This time, it took him just one day to back down. Here we go again. Ever since the US and Israel launched their latest war on Iran on 28 February, the people of the planet have been subjected to Donald Trump’s on-again off-again relationship with raining down catastrophic destruction on the nation. It started on 21 March, when Trump promised to hit Iranian power plants (a war crime, incidentally) unless Iran opened the strait of Hormuz. He delayed that plan for five days, and then another 10 days, before issuing his next threat. That was on 7 April, when he wrote: “A whole civilization will die tonight, never to be brought back again.” A mere 10 hours later, he walked back that (genocidal) threat. On 17 May, he wrote: “For Iran, the Clock is Ticking, and they better get moving, FAST, or there won’t be anything left of them. TIME IS OF THE ESSENCE!” On 18 May, he wrote that he had been asked by Gulf leaders to “hold off on our planned Military attack of the Islamic Republic of Iran, which was scheduled for tomorrow”. The approach seems as tedious as it does childish, constantly threatening one thing only to back down in a cringey, face-saving effort shortly thereafter. Let’s call it what it is: kindergarten diplomacy. From appearances, it would seem that Trump considers this a strategy. One can only assume he holds out hope that it will achieve an end to this catastrophic conflagration he and Benjamin Netanyahu began. The war is a massive failure, plunging his popularity along with American regional dominance in the Middle East. What’s clear is that Trump hasn’t a clue about how to exit a war he never should have started in the first place. Leadership is needed when difficult decisions must be made, but Trump is not capable of such resolve. Instead, he seems primarily driven to make pronouncements based on the last person he talked to. When Netanyahu visited him in the Oval Office on 21 July, the Israeli prime minister discussed three options for the war with Trump, according to reports: “a (negotiated) deal, continuing the blockade and economic pressures, and a massive strike”, is how a senior Israeli official described the meeting to Reuters. (Let’s not forget that Netanyahu helped convince Trump to start this war back in February.) Two days later, Trump threatened a massive strike (then called it off, then threatened it again). When the president’s threat reappeared, Saudi Arabia’s Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman called Trump on 1 August to argue for de-escalation. Guess what? To no one’s surprise, Trump backed down again. Nixon had his madman theory, in which he sought to project an image of himself as unhinged and irrational to frighten the Soviet Union into concessions. Trump, whether he knows it or not, is turning indecision into his own presidential doctrine. Such indecision is probably in part a reflection of Trump’s unflagging desire to please influential people around him. Trump’s deep-seated need to be liked by those he perceives to be powerful or popular (see: Trump’s meeting with Zohran Mamdani) is, I think, often underappreciated. But there is more behind Trump’s indecision as well. This administration cannot make any of the necessary decisions on Iran because it, along with Trump’s Maga base and the larger Republican party, has been split, as if by a lightning bolt, by the question. Vice-President JD Vance has been the most skeptical in the president’s inner circle of the war. Ever aware of the political winds, the vice-president is said to be carefully watching the rising rightwing criticism of Israel, due in part to this war. Vance went on the popular podcast The Joe Rogan Experience in mid-July and claimed that there was an Israeli government campaign to shape popular opinion in the US about the war. “There are some people within their system, we know beyond a shadow of a doubt, who are manipulating and trying to change American public opinion to keep the war going on indefinitely,” he said. “Not toward any objective, but just indefinitely.” Ever the faithful lieutenant to Trump, Marco Rubio, on the other hand, told Lara Trump on Fox News that the Iranian regime “has never faced a president like President Trump, which is someone that actually takes action”. Trump’s son-in-law and US negotiator Jared Kushner (along with Vance and their fellow negotiator Steve Witkoff) favors reducing the conflict, thereby lowering gas prices and limiting the danger to US armed forces, but just until after the midterm elections, when the war could potentially be ramped up again, according to Israel Hayom. The chairperson of the joint chiefs of staff, Gen Dan Caine, who counseled the president against the war in the first place, is now warning that stockpiles for air defense interceptors are dangerously low due to the war in Iran, putting the men and women in the US military at greater risk. Meanwhile, the Memorandum of Understanding that the US signed with Iran in June has been the subject of fierce Republican opposition, with the Louisiana Republican senator Bill Cassidy calling it “the worst foreign policy blunder in decades”. Even Trump loyalists such as the Texas senator Ted Cruz criticized the memorandum, saying: “The president is receiving some very poor advice on this deal.” And the Maga faithful have grown cold on the war, with only about a third of its voters believing the war is worth the economic cost, according to a Politico poll. Add to this the fact that CNN is now reporting that US military leadership is basically out of ideas about how to proceed with Iran at this point and is soliciting, via a crowdsourcing-type email sent to a group of military analysts, “new creative and unconventional ways to pressure and punish Iran”. The report also explains that Trump “has been considering strikes akin to a ‘fireworks’ display’”, which would suggest “a symbolic victory that would allow him to exit the war without actually accomplishing one of his initial aims: ridding Iran of its nuclear program”. Charting a course through the stormy winds of political decision making is what presidents must do all the time. A debacle like the war in Iran, begun with a terrible decision and bringing much unnecessary harm to the people of the region, must eventually be followed by a brave one, however painful it is to this nation or its leadership. A responsible president would make such a choice, even when difficult, and explain the reasoning to the nation. We, unfortunately, do not have serious leaders. And so we are left with kindergarten diplomacy. Moustafa Bayoumi is the author of the award-winning books How Does It Feel To Be a Problem?: Being Young and Arab in America and This Muslim American Life: Dispatches from the War on Terror. He is professor of English at Brooklyn College, City University of New York, and a Guardian US columnist

webTitle: ‘If we don’t fight back, we don’t have a future’: the journalist taking on the ‘tech fascists’ of Silicon Valley

fields.headline: ‘If we don’t fight back, we don’t have a future’: the journalist taking on the ‘tech fascists’ of Silicon Valley
fields.trailText: As Elon Musk, Peter Thiel and their peers have grown richer and more influential, Gil Durán argues they have all but abandoned democracy – and found the perfect government to enable them
fields.bodyText: In April, Gil Durán was permanently banned from Elon Musk’s X for posting just two words. Durán was responding to a post from the tech company Palantir outlining its 22‑point “technological manifesto”, which praised American “hard power”, western culture and AI weapons, denounced inclusivity and called for compulsory national service. Durán responded: “TLDR: Fascism” (TLDR is short for “too long, didn’t read”). Durán didn’t break any of X’s written rules, he points out over a video call from San Francisco – so much for Musk’s “free-speech absolutism”. His ban might just have had something to do with his preceding tweet, showing the cover of his new book, The Nerd Reich: Silicon Valley Fascism and the War on Democracy. The book’s central argument is that big tech is no longer our friend, as many of its billionaire owners have seized economic and political control and are steering the fate of the planet towards their own bizarre, apocalyptic visions. Fascism is no exaggeration, Durán asserts. He researched multiple definitions – by Umberto Eco, Robert Paxton, Jason Stanley – and decided that Donald Trump’s Make America Great Again (Maga) movement ticks all the boxes. “It’s a cult of grievance that seeks to purge its enemies by demonising them through absurd and surreal propaganda that exploits fears over law and order and gender and sexuality in order to seize power and install a permanent hierarchy that fascists consider the moral order of the world and the universe. In addition, you also have this sort of nationalistic, militaristic vibe.” By extension, he says, Silicon Valley is fascist “because they have wholly aligned with a fascist movement. That’s their vehicle for gaining power.” Few could dispute this alignment after seeing the bosses of Meta, Google, Apple, Amazon and OpenAI line up behind Trump at his second inauguration, or Musk’s now shuttered “department of government efficiency” (Doge) being given free rein to conduct mass firings of federal employees, or Palantir’s AI-driven surveillance technology enabling deportations by Immigration and Customs Enforcement. It’s a cosy relationship, Durán says: the tech titans have helped Trump and his family become billionaires through cryptocurrency and have been given government contracts and freedom from regulation or oversight. In addition, Durán believes, “Silicon Valley has gone fascist because they have adopted an extreme ideology of tech supremacy.” While Maga promises a return to a mythical glorious past, he says, the “technofascists” are promising a mythical glorious future: “We’re going to be in the stars. We’re going to be in space. And all we need is to get rid of anybody who stands in our way as we seek to accelerate technology toward this speedy, violent, God-like transcendence that we will achieve if we can only burn enough energy and enough compute to bring our boom loop into existence.” It sounds almost like a conspiracy theory, but Durán is not short of evidence. Musk making an apparent Nazi salute and describing empathy as “the fundamental weakness of western civilisation”. Palantir’s Peter Thiel writing in 2009 that “I no longer believe that freedom and democracy are compatible” and giving a lecture series suggesting Greta Thunberg could be the antichrist. Marc Andreessen, the CEO of the tech investment company Andreessen Horowitz, paraphrasing Filippo Tommaso Marinetti, the co-author of Mussolini’s Fascist Manifesto, in his “Techno-Optimist Manifesto”: “Technology must be a violent assault on the forces of the unknown, to force them to bow before man.” Durán, a journalist and former political adviser, lays out the narrative in exacting detail, outlining the connections between these men (and it is all men) and the origins of their often deeply weird beliefs, many of which view everyone outside their circle or opposed to their agenda as expendable. Unpacking all their overlapping philosophies would take some time, but TLDR: “It’s the idea that what matters more is the billions or trillions of people yet unborn in the future. And the only way they’re going to get to be born is if this elite group of white tech figures and gazillionaires makes the right decisions to make the human race transhuman and multiplanetary through AI and technology,” says Durán. “By becoming a billionaire, they all have this idea that they’re superior to everyone else. They are susceptible to this kind of thinking.” Durán, 50, is almost the opposite: the son of working-class Mexican immigrants in California. He was the first in his family to go to college, having grown up in relative poverty: “It made me tough and gave me an unyielding loyalty to regular people over the many rich and powerful people I’ve spent a lot of my time around.” Durán’s book traces the roots of this movement to two important sources. One is the 1997 book The Sovereign Individual, written by the American investor James Dale Davidson and William Rees-Mogg, the former Times editor and BBC grandee (and father of Jacob). Their book prophesied how digital tools such as the internet and cryptocurrency would pave the way for a privatised, corporatised, unregulated, post-democratic future ruled by rich, powerful, unaccountable individuals. Two decades later, this led to the idea of “network states” – digital realms beyond the jurisdiction of nation states – as popularised by Balaji Srinivasan, a former partner at Andreessen Horowitz. The other source is Curtis Yarvin, a former software developer and armchair philosopher with a penchant for psychedelics, sometimes referred to as the godfather of the “dark enlightenment”. In pseudonymous blogs in the late 2000s, Yarvin outlined a worldview in which liberal democracy had failed to deliver progress, partly because institutions such as education and the media had been captured by what he called “the Cathedral”. His proposed solution was a mass firing of government employees (he coined the acronym “Rage”, “retire all government employees”) and the installation of a “national CEO, [or] what’s called a dictator”. Yarvin also mused about a “humane alternative to genocide” to deal with unproductive citizens and has had to deny accusations that he is a white supremacist or supports racist ideologies. Scratch the surface, Durán suggests, and Yarvin’s ideas have much in common with Nazi ideologies, “but updated as rightwing dogma for the blogging age”. Both of these sources might have languished in obscurity had it not been for Thiel, the man at the heart of Silicon Valley’s rightward lurch. He has amassed enormous wealth through a series of investments in tech startups – first PayPal, then Facebook, Spotify, LinkedIn, Palantir and OpenAI, among others. He was the first major tech figure to back Donald Trump, in July 2016, and persuaded others to follow, including Andreessen, who said he spent half his time at Mar-a-Lago in the month after Trump won the 2024 election. Thiel liked The Sovereign Individual so much that he wrote a new introduction when it was reprinted in 2020. He has also made steps to found his own network state – first via the ill-fated “seasteading” movement (establishing floating countries in international waters) then via Próspera, a “special economic zone” on an island in Honduras. Incorporated in 2017 with permission from the Honduran government and reportedly co-funded by Srinivasan, Andreessen and OpenAI’s Sam Altman, Próspera has sought to attract digital startups with loose regulations (appealing to longevity researchers), low taxes and a crypto-friendly economy. Other similar projects have sprung up. In 2021, the president of El Salvador, Nayib Bukele, hailed the mooted creation of a “Bitcoin City”. In 2023, Trump announced plans to build 10 “Freedom Cities” on government land across the US, with input from Próspera representatives. In 2024, Srinivasan founded a “Network School” in Johor, Malaysia. Thiel also began to absorb Yarvin’s theories about how the political order was preventing progress. In the 2009 essay in which Thiel declared the incompatibility of freedom and democracy, he also said “the vast increase in welfare beneficiaries and the extension of the franchise to women” made capitalist democracy impossible, which did not win him many mainstream supporters. But Yarvin backed up Thiel and the two became friends and allies. “While The Sovereign Individual provided the foundation for the billionaire’s political vision, Yarvin created a blueprint for turning that vision into reality,” Durán writes. Thiel was instrumental in injecting these ideas, and people, into the US government – not least JD Vance, whom Durán describes as “almost entirely a creation of Peter Thiel”. It was Thiel who set up Vance as a venture capitalist, giving him a role at his firm Mithril Capital, then investing in Vance’s own fund, Narya Capital (Tolkien-derived names are a theme with these people). It was Thiel who backed Vance’s move into politics, where he went from condemning Trump as “America’s Hitler” to supporting him and parroting Yarvin’s ideas. “I think that what Trump should do, if I was giving him one piece of advice: fire every single mid-level bureaucrat, every civil servant in the administrative state, replace them with our people,” Vance told the podcaster Jack Murphy in 2021. Durán had observed this Silicon Valley takeover developing and began writing about it in 2024. “I thought this would be a problem in five to 10 years, but when JD Vance got on the ticket, it suddenly took on a new urgency,” he says. Now, it almost feels too late. In 2025, Bloomberg reported that at least 16 men connected to Thiel and his companies occupied positions of power in the Trump administration, including David Sacks, who is now a special adviser for AI and crypto. Musk’s Doge has swung its chainsaw at the government, crypto and AI regulation has all but disappeared, the Trump family are now billionaires and the tech oligarchs have become the Republicans’ largest donors. At the same time, they have become substantial beneficiaries of the very government they once sought to dismantle. Palantir has an estimated $13.7bn in US government contracts; last year, its stock price rose more than 90% in six months. Andreessen is backing dozens of defence companies scooping up government contracts and recently joined the Pentagon’s advisory board. Last week, Musk’s SpaceX received a $1.6bn contract to supply rockets to the US Space Force – on the same day he pledged at least $100m to help Republicans in November’s midterm elections. “It’s a severe cautionary tale about the hazards of privatisation,” says Durán. “The government created these men, especially Elon Musk. And now these welfare kings want to pull up the ladder, want to destroy the very system that made them. This is a massive failure by the US intelligence apparatus – to not see this threat forming from the inside.” Durán, who worked in communications for Kamala Harris when she was California’s attorney general, as well as for the late Democratic senator Dianne Feinstein, blames the Democrats as much as the Republicans. “They have failed tremendously to stand up to billionaire power because the only people as addicted to billionaire money in American politics as the Republicans are the Democrats,” he says. He singles out the California governor, Gavin Newsom, as a prime example of a “Silicon Valley Democrat”: “You don’t see him criticising these guys. He only goes after Trump, Trump, Trump and Vance, Vance, Vance … You want some viral content? Why don’t you go off on Peter Thiel’s weird antichrist obsession?” Even if the Democrats take control after the midterms or the 2028 presidential election, Durán is worried that “these tech fascists will win … because Democrats will not hold them accountable”. On the plus side, the Silicon Valley takeover has not been going that well lately. Network states around the world are losing ground. In 2021, Próspera’s special economic status was repealed by the new president, Xiomara Castro (it is suing the Honduran government for $10.8bn). Two weeks ago, Srinivasan’s Network School was ordered to close (Srinivasan says he is moving it to Kazakhstan). Trump’s Freedom Cities remain unbuilt. One saving grace, says Durán, is that “a lot of these people don’t really have a great grasp of on-the-ground realities”. Nobody really wants to live in a soulless network state, he says: “Why would you be in Kazakhstan instead of San Francisco, which is the global capital of tech?” On the other hand, he points out, the tech billionaires have effectively turned the US into a de facto network state. But they may well have overplayed their hand. “Silicon Valley oligarchs are really vulnerable right now,” says Durán. “People don’t like them. People are starting to rise up against data centres and this vision of an AI apocalypse that kills all the jobs and potentially kills all of humanity. You’re scaring the hell out of people and now they don’t like you. Into that could step a politician to take advantage of that trend and come up with a message that speaks to the concerns of people and against the dark fantasies of the oligarchs.” The question now, he says, “is how we turn the momentum in our favour and against the billionaires. Because they have a plan to win. They think they’re going to succeed.” This could be a radicalising moment: “In fighting against billionaire power, we find the key to all of our problems. Every moment is an important opportunity to wake people up and to start to fight back.” If not, he says, we’ll find ourselves in a situation where “we don’t have democracy, we don’t have an economy and we don’t have a future. If that doesn’t radicalise people, then we deserve what we’re going to get.” • The Nerd Reich: Silicon Valley Fascism and the War on Democracy is published on 18 August (Simon & Schuster, £25). webTitle: El-Sayed holds narrow lead in Michigan Senate primary but race too close to call

fields.headline: El-Sayed holds narrow lead in Michigan Senate primary but race too close to call
fields.trailText: Abdul El-Sayed and his opponent Haley Stevens were both optimistic late in the evening
fields.bodyText: The marquee race for the Democratic nomination for Senate in Michigan remained too close to call on Tuesday night, with Abdul El-Sayed, a progressive former public health official, holding a narrow lead over congresswoman Haley Stevens. The battleground state is crucial to the party’s hopes of winning back control of the Senate in November’s midterm elections. The winner of Tuesday’s Democratic primary will face the Republican nominee, former representative Mike Rogers, in November, to succeed the retiring Democratic senator Gary Peters. As ballot counting continued into the early hours of Wednesday morning, hundreds of restless El-Sayed supporters remained at the election watch party at the Majestic Theater in Detroit, as his lead over Stevens remained at a few percentage points. At about 4am local time, El-Sayed had 48.7% of the vote and Stevens 47.3%, with 95% counted, according to the Associated Press. In remarks to supporters, El-Sayed turned his attention from the contentious primary against Stevens to the Republican nominee. He called for the party to unite against Rogers, who he assailed as a “corporate sellout” who “should never see the inside of the US senate”. “We’re going to have to wait a little longer to see the outcome of this race,” El-Sayed said, “but as I look in front of me, I already see the outcome.” Hasan Piker, the streamer and new Democratic kingmaker, as well as the Democratic nominee for Philadelphia’s third district, Chris Rabb, and the Democratic nominee for Colorado’s 1st district, Melat Kiros, were among the crowd listening to El-Sayed speak at length about his American story as the son of Egyptian immigrants. With 13 weeks left before November, El-Sayed argued that however much his supporters may disagree with his Democratic opponent, there was more uniting the left than dividing it. “However we might feel about the campaign we’ve just come through, I want you to understand that it pales in comparison to the cynicism, in comparison to the corporatism, in comparison to the lies that Mike Rogers and Donald Trump are going to tell,” he said. Nearby, at the Hotel Saint Regis, an upbeat Stevens told supporters at her election night event that results may not come until later Wednesday morning. “We knew that this was going to be a close race, and that’s exactly what we’ve got,” she said. “But friends,” she said to loud cheers from the room, “I am feeling good about this race.” El-Sayed, 41, built a grassroots campaign statewide on a message of universal healthcare and getting money out of politics. Stevens, 43, cast herself as a pragmatic problem-solver, and saw her campaign boosted by tens of millions of dollars in outside spending, including from groups affiliated with the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (Aipac), the pro-Israel lobbying organization. Rogers, a former Michigan congressman who was also the Republican nominee for Senate in 2024 when he lost to Elissa Slotkin, ran unopposed in the Republican primary. Mallory McMorrow, a Democrat who dropped out of Michigan’s Democratic primary race in July, said it was vital for the party to come together after a bruising campaign to help the ticket win in November. “I voted for great Democrats up and down the ballot, and I made a commitment that whoever wins the Senate race tonight, I will be endorsing as soon as that race is called,” she told CNN. “I will be headed to their election night party to show we all come together after whatever happens tonight, so that we can be a team as we head in November.” McMorrow later endorsed El-Sayed. “Abdul has my full endorsement and support,” she wrote on social media. “This was a brutal primary (believe me, I know). And Trump and Mike Rogers are counting on us staying divided. Let’s prove them wrong by beating Mike Rogers and taking our country back.” With ballots still being counted, the results in Michigan – and in four other states holding elections, including Kansas, Missouri, Virginia and Washington state – were coming into focus. Jocelyn Benson, the Democratic secretary of state, will face John James, a Donald Trump-endorsed congressman, in the state’s open governor’s race after Gretchen Whitmer faced term limits. James has denied the results of the 2020 election where Joe Biden won; most recently, alongside Trump at a rally, James claimed Trump had won Michigan “three times”. In Michigan’s seventh congressional district, progressive organizer William Lawrence beat out two more moderate candidates, former US ambassador to Ukraine Bridget Brink and Matt Maasdam, a former US Navy Seal. Lawrence secured an endorsement from Bernie Sanders, the progressive Vermont senator. A challenge to the incumbent representative Shri Thanedar in Michigan’s 13th district by Detroit state representative Donavan McKinney remained too close to call. In Missouri and Washington state, the Democratic establishment struck back, blunting a string of progressive victories. In Missouri’s first congressional district, the Democratic congressman Wesley Bell defeated the progressive former representative Cori Bush in a rematch for the St Louis-based seat. Bush had sought to make the contest a referendum on pro-Israel spending and the war in Gaza. “When we think about all of the division that we hear, I think it is important that we focus on what this place can be,” Bell said after his race was called. Meanwhile, in Washington’s third congressional district, blue dog representative Marie Gluesenkamp Perez fended off a progressive challenger in her battleground district, prevailing in a crowded all-party primary. She will face Republican John Braun in November. Missouri voters also rejected an amendment that would have required citizens’ initiatives to pass in all congressional districts rather than by a simple statewide majority. In Kansas, state senator Cindy Holscher won the Democratic nomination in the gubernatorial race, beating two other politicians to advance to the general election. And in Virginia, Shannon Taylor won in the first congressional district and Elaine Luria won in the second congressional district, in wins for moderate Democrats.

webTitle: Michigan’s high-stakes Democratic primary for US Senate seat too close to call – as it happened

fields.headline: Michigan’s high-stakes Democratic primary for US Senate seat too close to call – as it happened
fields.trailText: This live blog is now closed.
fields.bodyText: The major Democratic contest for Michigan’s US Senate nomination remains too close to call. About two-thirds of the votes throughout the state have been counted, with Abdul El‑Sayed, an epidemiologist and former public health official, is just three points ahead of establishment‑backed Haley Stevens, a US congresswoman. Also in Michigan, Jocelyn Benson clinched the Democratic nomination in the governor’s race and will face the John James, who won the Republican contest. Benson, the state’s secretary of state, will take on James, a congressman who received Donald Trump’s endorsement, to replace the term-limited Democratic governor, Gretchen Whitmer, in November. Further down ballot, William Lawrence, a progressive, won a competitive three-way Democratic primary race in Michigan’s seventh congressional district. Lawrence, a community organizer who co-founded the Sunrise Movement, will now challenge Republican incumbent Tom Barrett, who has bucked his own party while in office, after he flipped the key battleground district red in 2024. Meanwhile in Washington state, Marie Gluesenkamp Perez, the two-term centrist Democrat, has advanced to the general election for her competitive US House seat. She’ll face the Republican candidate and state senator, John Braun, who is backed by Trump. The state votes on single ballots – meaning the top two finishers, regardless of party, advance to November’s contest. More here. And in Missouri, Democratic congressman Wesley Bell won his primary in the St Louis area on Tuesday, ending the progressive former representative Cori Bush’s bid for a comeback. Bell’s victory blunted the momentum pro-Palestinian candidates have shown in recent elections. In this deep-blue district, this also makes Bell the favorite to win a second term in the November election. More here. Also in the midwest, Cindy Holscher, a state senator, won the Democratic nomination in Kansas’s gubernatorial race. She beat two other Sunflower state politicians to advance to the general election. Ty Masterson, the Trump-backed Kansas state senate president, clinched the GOP nomination in a crowded race. It’s set to be a fierce competition, as Republicans are angling to retake the governor’s mansion from Democratic control. With a little more than 60% of the vote counted in Michigan’s marquee Senate primary race, the insurgent Democratic candidate Abdul El‑Sayed, an epidemiologist and former public health official, is just three points ahead of establishment‑backed Haley Stevens, a US congresswoman. According to the Associated Press, El‑Sayed is posting strong numbers in Washtenaw county, home to Ann Arbor and the University of Michigan, and in Kent county, which includes Grand Rapids. Stevens, meanwhile, is ahead in Oakland county, which covers many of Detroit’s northern suburbs. Only 48% of the vote has been counted in Wayne county, Michigan’s largest.
